Family Health

Bone-density scans: preparing for DXA and understanding the result

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A bone-density scan, often called DXA or DEXA, uses a small amount of X-ray radiation to measure bone mineral density. It helps clinicians assess osteoporosis and fracture risk and, when appropriate, monitor treatment. The result is one part of a bone-health assessment rather than a prediction that a particular bone will break.

What the scan measures

Central DXA usually measures the hip and lower spine. In selected circumstances, the forearm is used. The result estimates mineral density; it does not measure every aspect of bone strength or explain why density is low.

Osteoporosis makes bones more vulnerable to fractures. Low bone density, sometimes called osteopenia, is less severe by the scan classification, but its significance depends on the person’s overall fracture risk.

A DXA examination is different from a nuclear-medicine bone scan, which uses an injected tracer for other questions. Portable heel or other peripheral tests also do not always replace a central DXA examination.

Who might be offered testing?

Age, menopause, previous low-trauma fractures, body weight, family history, certain medicines and underlying illnesses can influence the decision. Long-term glucocorticoid use and some hormone-related conditions may justify assessment outside routine screening ages.

In the United States, the USPSTF recommends screening women from age 65 and younger postmenopausal women whose clinical risk assessment indicates increased risk. Its evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against routine screening in men. That does not mean a man with risk factors should never be tested.

Other professional guidelines and countries use different criteria, including age-based testing for some men. Follow your local pathway and individual risk assessment rather than treating a single age threshold as universal.

Tell your clinician about a fracture after a minor fall, new back pain or noticeable height loss. These may need assessment for vertebral fractures or other conditions, not just a future routine scan.

Low activity, smoking, heavy alcohol use and inadequate calcium or vitamin D can contribute to bone-health risk. Hip, spine and wrist fractures after relatively minor trauma are especially useful history to report. Some professional groups recommend testing men from age 70, but eligibility differs from the USPSTF population-screening recommendation.

Preparing for the appointment

The imaging centre will provide instructions. You can usually eat normally, but may be asked to avoid calcium supplements for at least 24 hours. Confirm the timing with the centre rather than stopping prescribed treatment for longer on your own.

Mention a recent barium examination, contrast-enhanced imaging or nuclear-medicine test because it can affect when DXA should be done. Wear comfortable clothing without metal over the area to be scanned, or change into the gown provided.

Tell the team if you are pregnant or pregnancy is possible. Routine DXA is usually postponed during pregnancy because it can generally wait. This precaution does not mean that any tiny radiation exposure inevitably harms a fetus.

What happens during DXA?

You lie on an open scanning table while the equipment passes over the relevant area. Your legs may be supported to position the spine, and your foot may be turned slightly for the hip measurement.

The scan itself is usually painless and does not involve an injection. You need to remain still; the operator may give short breathing instructions. Let them know if pain or limited movement makes the position difficult.

The appointment is generally brief, and you can usually return to normal activities afterwards. Ask who will explain the report and when to expect it.

Understanding T-scores

A T-score compares bone density with a healthy young-adult reference population. More negative numbers mean lower density relative to that reference. The usual categories apply to postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or over at appropriate measurement sites.

A T-score of −1.0 or higher is in the normal range. A score below −1.0 but above −2.5 is low bone density. A score of −2.5 or lower meets the bone-density threshold for osteoporosis in the relevant population.

The direction matters: −3.0 is lower than −2.5. A score of −0.1 is not the cutoff for normal density. A number close to a boundary still needs interpretation with scan quality, fracture history and the rest of your assessment.

Why younger people may receive a Z-score

For premenopausal women and men under 50, a Z-score is generally preferred. It compares density with an age-matched reference rather than a young-adult reference.

A Z-score of −2.0 or lower is described as below the expected range for age. It does not automatically diagnose osteoporosis on its own. Children need their own assessment criteria, including growth and fracture history.

Hormonal treatment and gender-related clinical circumstances can also affect reporting choices. Ask the clinician which reference and diagnostic criteria are appropriate for you.

Deciding what to do next

A clinician may combine the scan with a fracture-risk calculator, previous fracture history and tests for causes of bone loss. Normal blood calcium does not by itself establish normal bone density.

Care may include adequate calcium and vitamin D, appropriate weight-bearing and resistance exercise, balance work, fall prevention and smoking cessation. If you already have fractures or osteoporosis, get advice on suitable exercise rather than starting high-impact activity indiscriminately.

Some people need medicines to lower fracture risk, including people whose risk is high despite a T-score above −2.5. Diet and exercise are valuable but do not replace indicated treatment.

Repeat scans should have a clinical purpose and an individually chosen interval. Small changes may reflect measurement variation. Comparable equipment and proper analysis help the team judge whether a change is real.

Suitable weight-bearing activities may include walking or dancing, with resistance work adapted to your condition. Blood tests for vitamin D, calcium or selected hormones may help investigate an underlying cause; they do not replace the density measurement.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Interpret DXA using the appropriate age and sex context, scan sites and fracture history.

A score alone does not determine treatment; risk factors and previous fragility fractures can change the plan.

How BeMama can help

Bring fracture and medicine history, ask which score applies to you, and confirm how the result changes your care.

When to seek help

Tell the scanning centre if pregnancy is possible; new severe back pain after minor trauma needs clinical assessment.

Sources and further reading

  • ISCD — Official Adult Positions

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • DXA measures bone density and contributes to fracture-risk assessment.
  • T-score cutoffs must use the correct negative signs and age context.
  • Z-scores are generally more appropriate before menopause and in men under 50.
  • Treatment decisions include fracture history and other risks, not the scan alone.

Frequently asked questions

Does low bone density mean a fracture is inevitable?

No. It is one risk factor. Age, previous fractures, falls, medicines and other conditions also influence risk.

Is −2.7 a better score than −2.3?

No. The more negative value represents lower density relative to the reference. In the appropriate adult population, −2.7 is below the osteoporosis threshold.

Must everyone repeat DXA every year?

No. The interval depends on the reason for testing, treatment and whether a new result would change management.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
